record.paper_title: A metal-insulator transition in 2D: Established facts and open questions
record.context_brief: Origin of large resistance changes deep in the metallic phase
record.original_question: What microscopic mechanism explains the large changes in resistance that are observed deep in the metallic phase of strongly correlated two-dimensional electron and hole systems, including the experimentally observed very large resistivity changes far from the critical region rather than only in the immediate vicinity of the metal-insulator transition?

evidence.quote: Therefore, although the theory of Punnoose and Finkelstein32,78 quantitatively describes experimental data in the close vicinity of the transition, it cannot explain the large effects observed far from the transition.

Although the behavior in the close vicinity of the transition is quantitatively described by the renormalization-group theory of Punnoose and Finkelstein32 without any fitting parameters, there is currently no microscopic theory that can explain the whole range of observed phenomena. The origin of the large changes in the resistance deep in the metallic phase remains unclear, with suggested explanations ranging from temperature-dependent screening72–76 to an analog of the Pomeranchuk effect.65–67

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a strongly correlated two-dimensional electron (or hole) system at low temperatures, in the regime of low carrier density where the dimensionless interaction parameter r_s (the ratio of the Coulomb interaction energy to the Fermi energy) is large. As a function of carrier density n, such systems display a metal-insulator transition (MIT) at a critical density n_c: for n > n_c the resistivity ρ(T) decreases as the temperature T is lowered (metallic behavior), while for n < n_c it increases (insulating behavior). In the immediate vicinity of n_c, the temperature and density dependence of ρ is quantitatively described, without fitting parameters, by the two-loop renormalization-group theory of interacting disordered electrons (Finkelstein-type theory), which treats the coupled flow of disorder and Fermi-liquid interaction amplitudes.

Experimentally, however, the resistivity exhibits very large changes (by factors of order 3–10 or more) as a function of temperature deep inside the metallic phase, at densities n significantly larger than n_c, where the renormalization-group theory predicts only weak variations and therefore fails to account for the observed magnitude of dρ/dT.

Problem: Provide a microscopic theory of transport in such strongly correlated, weakly disordered two-dimensional electron and hole systems that quantitatively explains the large temperature-dependent resistivity changes observed deep in the metallic phase (far from the critical region), and that reduces, near the critical density, to the established renormalization-group description of the metal-insulator transition. Candidate mechanisms to be evaluated or surpassed include temperature-dependent screening of charged impurities by the two-dimensional carriers and a Pomeranchuk-like entropy mechanism associated with localized magnetic moments; the desired theory should specify the dominant scattering processes, predict ρ(T, n) in the full metallic regime, and connect smoothly to the critical behavior at n → n_c.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent reviews and research on strongly correlated 2D electron systems continue to describe the origin of the large temperature-dependent resistivity deep in the metallic phase as not fully resolved. The Punnoose–Finkelstein renormalization-group theory remains the quantitative description near the critical region, while explanations for the deep-metallic regime (temperature-dependent screening, Pomeranchuk-like effects, incipient ferromagnetism) remain competing without a unified microscopic theory.

status_evidence.title: Metal–insulator transition and low-density phases in a strongly-interacting two-dimensional electron system
status_evidence.snippet: The driving force behind the MIT is strong correlations between carriers; a quantum critical point separates an interaction-stabilized metal from a disorder-dominated insulator.
status_evidence.claim: A unified microscopic explanation across the full metallic regime is still being developed; reviews continue to frame this as an open issue.

status_evidence.title: Metal-insulator transitions, Imada et al., Rev. Mod. Phys.
status_evidence.snippet: Comprehensive review of metal-insulator transitions emphasizing the interplay of interactions and disorder; no single microscopic theory covers all observed transport phenomena in 2D strongly correlated systems.
status_evidence.claim: No microscopic theory yet covers the full range of resistivity behavior across the 2D MIT, supporting open status.
